There’s more than one way to expand your reach in the aftermarket.

- Business Growth: A Constant Risk vs. Opportunity Calculation

- New Technology Reshapes Aftermarket Parts and Service Demand

- ADAS Complexity Reshapes Aftermarket Product Strategy

A company can add locations, enter new markets and build its distribution network over time. It can also acquire an established business or partner with a network that already has the relationships and infrastructure in place.

Recent aftermarket moves show both approaches in action. Parts Authority acquired NPW Companies, while Dana expanded its relationship with VIPAR Heavy Duty. STILLEN also joined The AAM Group as a supporting supplier partner.

The deals vary in size and structure, but they have something in common: Each gives the companies involved an opportunity to reach more of the aftermarket through an established network.

Expanding Through Acquisition

NPW brought 46 locations to Parts Authority, increasing the combined network to nearly 325 locations. The acquisition also expanded Parts Authority’s reach into five new states.

That kind of growth would take considerable time to build location by location. Through the acquisition, Parts Authority gains an existing footprint, along with the infrastructure and customer relationships NPW has developed.

NPW also brings a broad portfolio of traditional, engine and performance parts. Its catalog includes more than 1 million part numbers from more than 700 brands. The acquisition adds product depth along with geographic reach.

For customers, a larger network can also put more inventory closer to the businesses that need it.

Reaching Customers Through Partnerships

Acquisition isn’t the only way to gain access to an established network.

Dana’s distribution agreement with VIPAR Heavy Duty will expand access to Dana’s commercial vehicle products across the VIPAR Heavy Duty Family of Companies network. The agreement will increase product availability for distributors, fleets and repair facilities across North America.

The agreement primarily focuses on Spicer drivetrain products and the Victor Reinz commercial vehicle sealing portfolio.

Instead of building that additional distribution footprint itself, Dana can use an established network to put its products within reach of more customers.

The approach differs from an acquisition, but the goal is similar: using an existing distribution footprint to expand market reach.

The STILLEN partnership with The AAM Group provides another variation.

STILLEN joined AAM as a supporting supplier partner for its Total Truck Centers and Parts Pro programs. The relationship connects STILLEN with a nationwide network of independent aftermarket businesses.

The partnership also goes beyond product availability. AAM will support STILLEN through email campaigns, customer promotions, digital marketing materials and training opportunities.

That highlights another role these networks can play. Suppliers need distribution, but they also need ways to provide product information and support to the businesses selling their products.

As the aftermarket continues to evolve, acquisitions and partnerships will remain two ways companies can strengthen their networks and reach new customers. The strategies may differ from one company to another, but distribution remains at the center. Ultimately, success still depends on connecting products, information and customers efficiently.

When customers request aggressive brake pads, the term can have several meanings. Some want sharper freeway stops. Others want more confidence on winding roads or greater control while towing. Some simply prefer a firmer and more responsive pedal.

- Continental Tire’s Brian Beierwaltes on Driving Brand Promise

- EV Safety: What You Need to Know

- Why Damaged O2 Sensors Cause More Problems Than You Think

Terms such as “aggressive,” “high performance,” and “racing” often appear in marketing. However, they do not always describe what the customer needs.

Technicians should begin by asking questions rather than recommending a product.

Ask About Current Brake Performance

The first question is: “What do you like or dislike about your current brakes?”

Long stopping distances, a soft pedal or inconsistent braking may not indicate a pad problem. Hydraulic faults, caliper issues or master cylinder problems can create similar symptoms.

Customers may incorrectly attribute those symptoms to the brake pads.

Technicians should also ask when the brakes were last serviced. A customer who cannot remember may not need a high-performance pad immediately.

In many cases, a premium replacement pad can restore like-new braking feel. This option may meet the customer’s needs without moving to a more aggressive product.

Define Expectations for Aggressive Brake Pads

The next question is: “What do you expect an aggressive brake pad to do?”

Advertising, online forums and articles may shape customer expectations before the visit. The technician’s role is to guide those expectations toward the correct application.

After identifying the customer’s preferences, ask how the vehicle operates each day. Determine whether it sees mostly highway driving, winding roads or stop-and-go traffic.

Also ask whether the customer regularly tows or hauls. These answers show how often the brakes experience heavy use.

They also indicate whether the brakes usually operate cold or at higher temperatures.

Discuss Noise, Dust and Pad Life

Technicians should explain potential differences in brake noise, dust, pedal feel and pad life. This discussion can prevent misunderstandings and avoidable comebacks.

A brake pad recommendation should follow the complete conversation. Some customers may already prefer a specific brand.

Others may rely on the technician’s recommendation. In either case, product research helps separate verified performance characteristics from marketing claims.

From our sister site, Tire Review.

CVSA releases 2026 Roadcheck results highlighting vehicle and driver violations

Roadcheck inspectors found 19% of commercial motor vehicles had out-of-service violations.

Cargo securement ranked fourth among North America’s top vehicle out-of-service violations.

Inspectors affixed 17,680 CVSA decals to vehicles that passed eligible safety inspections.

The Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance (CVSA) recently released the results of its 2026 International Roadcheck , with inspectors conducting 54,575 commercial motor vehicle and driver inspections across North America during the three-day event. The results show that 81% of vehicles and 94.2% of drivers inspected had no out-of-service (OOS) violations.

The alliance reported that inspectors placed 10,350 vehicles and 3,184 drivers OOS. Inspectors also affixed 17,680 CVSA decals to eligible vehicles that passed comprehensive safety inspections without critical mechanical or OOS violations.

Vehicle inspection results

Inspectors conducted 44,047 Level I, II, and V vehicle inspections and identified 13,924 OOS vehicle violations. Brake systems were the most frequently cited violation, with 3,379 violations accounting for 24.3% of all vehicle out-of-service violations.

Tires ranked second with 2,914 violations, followed by 20% defective brakes with 2,072. Cargo securement ranked fourth with 1,724 violations, while lights accounted for 1,659.

Combining brake systems and defective brakes, there were 5,451 total brake-related violations.

Cargo securement was the vehicle violation focus for this year’s Roadcheck. Inspectors identified violations involving freight that was inadequately restrained, immobilized, locked, secured, tied down, packed, or monitored.

Driver inspection results

Inspectors conducted 53,271 Level I, II, and III inspections involving commercial motor vehicle drivers. A total of 3,184 drivers were placed OOS.

The most common driver out-of-service violation was not having a medical card, accounting for 1,072 violations, or 27% of all driver out-of-service violations. Hours-of-service (HOS) violations ranked second with 929, followed by no commercial driver’s license with 620.

English language proficiency (ELP) violations accounted for 361 driver out-of-service violations, while false records of duty status accounted for 266.

ELD tampering, falsification, or manipulation was the driver violation focus for 2026. Inspectors issued 146 out-of-service orders for ELD tampering, making it the seventh most-cited driver OOS violation in North America.

CVSA releases 2026 human trafficking awareness results to strengthen prevention efforts

CVSA schedules Brake Safety Week for August 23–29 to improve brake compliance

Hazardous materials inspections

Inspectors conducted 2,590 inspections of vehicles transporting hazardous materials or dangerous goods (HM/DG). Those inspections resulted in 368 vehicle and 63 driver OOS violations.

Placarding was the top HM/DG out-of-service violation, with 40 violations accounting for 28.4% of all HM/DG OOS violations. Loading violations ranked second with 38, followed by shipping papers with 25.

What this means for the trucking industry

The 2026 Roadcheck results point fleets toward several areas that warrant continued attention, particularly brakes, tires, cargo securement, driver credentials, HOS, and ELD records.

The concentration of brake-related violations also reinforces the value of thorough preventive maintenance and pre-trip inspections. For fleet managers, the ELD findings show that compliance extends beyond having the required technology in the cab—accurate records and proper use remain critical.

The results also give fleets a practical checklist for preparing vehicles and drivers for roadside inspections, with mechanical condition, documentation, cargo securement, and electronic logging practices all affecting compliance.

The AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety’s newly released 2025 American Driving Survey shows gas and diesel vehicles continued to account for most driving in 2025 at 89.5% of all trips, down from 91% in 2024.

However, a research brief states that hybrid and electric vehicle use did increase last year, representing 7.4% (up 1% from 2024) and 3.1% of trips (up 0.6% from 2024), respectively.

AAA Foundation says the survey is meant to quantify the U.S. population’s daily driving and compare the results with previous years. A research brief explores trends in driving behavior by vehicle age and vehicle type, including differences across population groups. The survey was conducted between Jan. 1, 2023, and Dec. 31, 2025.

U.S. drivers collectively made 232 billion trips, spent 95 billion hours driving, and traveled 2.76 trillion miles last year.

Those results were projected to the national population based on a survey of 5,100 participants whose answers showed they made an average of 2.40 driving trips per day, spent 59.3 minutes driving, and traveled 28.6 miles daily.

“Driving patterns in 2025 remained similar to those observed in previous years, with only observed changes in travel exposure and vehicle characteristics,” the brief states. “Drivers traveled slightly fewer miles and spent slightly less time driving compared with 2024, while newer vehicles and vehicles with hybrid or electric powertrains continued to represent a growing share of trips. EV use remained limited but was associated with longer trips compared with conventional vehicles. Continued monitoring of travel behavior, vehicle characteristics, and demographic differences remains important for understanding changes in mobility patterns and their implications for traffic safety in the United States.”

Researchers found that 95% of U.S. residents ages 16 and older reported driving at least occasionally in 2025, a slight increase from 2024.

As in previous years, drivers ages 35–49 reported the most daily trips, driving time, and mileage, while drivers ages 16–19 reported the least, according to the brief.

“Driving prevalence increased across most age groups between 2024 and 2025,” the brief states. “The largest significant increase was observed among 16- to 19-year-olds, rising from 83.1% to 91.4%, and for 25- to 34-year-olds (95.5%). Smaller increases were observed across the remaining age groups, with driving rates exceeding 90% for all age categories.”

“Male drivers reported more trips, driving time, and miles than female drivers. “Drivers in the South reported the highest daily driving time and mileage, while drivers in the West reported the lowest. “Drivers with a bachelor’s degree or higher reported more trips and greater driving time and mileage than other education groups. “The distribution of driving trips by vehicle age continued to shift toward newer vehicles, with vehicles aged 0–4 years accounting for the largest share of trips (39.3%), up from 34% in 2024 and 27% in 2023.”

“Male drivers reported more trips, driving time, and miles than female drivers.

“Drivers in the South reported the highest daily driving time and mileage, while drivers in the West reported the lowest.

“Drivers with a bachelor’s degree or higher reported more trips and greater driving time and mileage than other education groups.

“The distribution of driving trips by vehicle age continued to shift toward newer vehicles, with vehicles aged 0–4 years accounting for the largest share of trips (39.3%), up from 34% in 2024 and 27% in 2023.”

AAA Foundation says that EV trips had the longest average duration and distance compared with gas/diesel and hybrid vehicles. Gas/diesel vehicles averaged 24.3 minutes and 11.8 miles per trip, while hybrids averaged 25 minutes and 12.4 miles.

EV trips had the longest average duration and distance, averaging 30.1 minutes and 13.8 miles per trip.

Hybrid and EV use was highest among drivers with a bachelor’s degree or higher and among drivers located in the West.

As for road trips, 30.1% of survey respondents reported taking at least one road trip in the previous four weeks, with an average one-way trip length of 234.8 miles. Gas/diesel vehicles remained the predominant vehicle type across all groups, accounting for more than 90% of trips in most categories.

NASHVILLE, Tenn. – TMD Friction has announced the launch of a new friction material for heavy-duty applications using air disc brakes. The new material is designated Textar T3080 and is engineered for applications where high torque levels are required to meet the FMVSS121 Stopping Distance Regulations. In addition, TMD says Textar T3080 already meets the 2014 and 2021 “Better Brakes Rules” environmental regulations for heavy metals and copper content, an upcoming challenge facing the brake friction industry. Multiple friction levels are required to best optimize pad and rotor life for different truck, tractor and trailer applications and T3080 rounds out Textar’s North American Air Disc Brake Friction product portfolio by adding a material for the most extreme torque applications on the road, TMD says. As the North American heavy truck market shifts more to air disc brakes, a key issue is the cost justification of this new brake product. Tom Green, managing director of TMD Friction North America noted, “If disc brakes are to replace drum brakes in large numbers, their acceptance will be based on initial and life cycle costs when compared to drum brakes. Disc brakes cost more upfront, so it is critical to maximize life and minimize operational costs. Textar now has four different friction materials for the North American air disc brake market. Each is designed to optimize the life cycle costs for a particular duty cycle.” Jim Clark, TMD’s director of engineering for NAFTA, added, “You don’t have to look far to find examples of multiple levels of brake lining friction to optimize brake life. Current drum brake linings on North American commercial vehicles have three distinct friction levels that rate at 20,000 lbs., 23,000 lbs., and the higher GAWRs. While the formulation, quality and consistency of any friction material product has a lot to do with its wear properties, a basic rule of friction science simply states, ‘the lower the friction, the longer the life of the friction material’. This also applies to the rotor. The lower the friction of the disc pad material, the longer the rotor will last. Besides improved life, having multiple friction levels is the best way to address brake balance problems the disc brake faces when mated to drum brakes. We have already seen disc/drum brake compatibility as an issue in working with several large fleets.” In dynamometer wear tests, two air disc friction materials with different effective coefficients of friction were tested by TMD. Results showed that with a higher effective coefficient of friction (0.38) the pad wears anywhere from 40 percent to 80 percent more than the lower friction pad (0.28). “Given the large difference in wear rates between the high and low ends of the typical friction range, it is important to select the appropriate friction level in order to maximize pad life, rotor life and maintain safety,” said Clark. “This is why TMD has developed multiple friction materials for North America, Textar – T3050, T3070 and T3080. They cover all the GAWR ratings. We also offer a special material, one of the European market leaders Textar T7400, for the transit bus and refuse truck market.”

https://www.bosch-presse.de/pressportal/.text: Stuttgart – Prof. Christof Ehrhart (60) is leaving Bosch on December 31, 2026, at his own request to pursue commitments and projects outside the company. In his capacity as the company’s head of communications, he has been responsible worldwide for internal and external communications, governmental affairs, relations with industry associations and stakeholder groups, and strategic brand management since 2019. Ehrhart can look back on three decades of leadership roles in international communications. In 2024, he received the prestigious German Image Award for the second time for his communications work at Bosch.

Stuttgart, Germany and Madrid, Spain – In Europe, pressure on urban public transit is mounting: in light of mandatory EU requirements to reduce carbon emissions from city buses by 90 percent by 2030, public transit operators are seeking reliable, emissions-free solutions. To this end, an initial test operation is now launching in Madrid: Equipped with a fuel-cell power module (FCPM) from Bosch, an Irizar bus has been transporting passengers through the Spanish capital for several weeks now. Vehicle operation will focus on routes where the fuel cell’s long range allows it to fully demonstrate its advantages. The operator is the Spanish bus company Alsa.

https://www.bosch-presse.de/pressportal/.text: Stuttgart – Bosch, in collaboration with Toyota Motor Europe, BMW Group and Repsol, today announces the launch of a pioneering six-month pilot project in Spain. The pilot, which started in early July, will demonstrate the real-world potential of Vehicles running Exclusively on Eligible Fuels (VEEF)*. The initiative will deploy a fleet of around 20 Toyota and BMW vehicles, powered by Repsol’s 100 % renewable gasoline (Nexa 95), and supported by Bosch’s advanced digital fuel tracking technology. This pilot aims to provide tangible, real-world evidence that vehicles exclusively running on eligible fuels can be effectively deployed at scale, supporting Europe’s transition to decarbonize mobility through a complementary, technology-neutral approach while leaving no one behind.
